title: Under the Scorching Sun
subtitle: The end of the Pacific War seen from Tokyo, Hiroshima, Nagasaki, Potsdam, Tinian and Washington, 1944–1945
intro: In the last eight months of the Pacific War, a remarkable number of people on both sides kept private records they were in no position to publish. Tokyo novelists hid diaries that would have cost them their freedom. A police photographer wrote up his night in the firestorm before he went out to photograph the dead. A Filipino diplomat serving Japan's client republic set down the explosions outside his window. On the other side of the Pacific, a president, his secretary of war and his commerce secretary each wrote a few lines at night about a weapon most of the world had never heard of. A young co-pilot on Tinian filled a notebook during the flight that used it.

This chapter places those voices side by side. The firebombing of Tokyo on the night of 9–10 March 1945 is seen by Ishikawa Kōyō, the Metropolitan Police photographer who nearly died in it, and by Uchida Hyakken, who watched refugees walk past in whatever they had on. Nagai Kafū lost his house and library that night. The medical student Yamada Fūtarō answered it with a cry for vengeance, and Leon Ma. Guerrero was woken by bombs just after midnight. Eleven weeks later, on 25–26 May, the raids came back for the rest of the city. Uchida, Yamada and the Diet's chief secretary Oki Misao were all burned out or fighting fires within the same few hours.

Then the eye moves outward. At Potsdam on 24–25 July, Henry Stimson pressed Truman again to spare Kyoto. Truman wrote that the bomb would hit only military objectives, never women and children. A fortnight later, Robert Lewis logged the release over Hiroshima, and less than a mile from the blast centre Dr. Hachiya Michihiko was stripped of his clothes and burned. The record for Nagasaki is thinner, and this chapter says so. The account used here was written ten years later by a pathologist who was not in the city. Henry Wallace's diary of 10 August records Truman stopping further atomic bombing.

On 15 August the eyes converge again, scattered now across a defeated country. In Kamakura, Takami Jun and Ōsaragi Jirō each heard the Emperor's broadcast under a blazing sun. In Okayama Prefecture, Tanizaki Jun'ichirō could not make out the radio and learned of the surrender from his weeping family. His refugee guest Kafū heard the news after a train ride and drank wine that evening to celebrate. In the mountains of Nagano, Yamada at first refused to believe it and then wept.

What these voices share is the gap between what each could see and what was happening. Kiyosawa Kiyoshi was sure defeat would bring violence. He died of pneumonia in May, three months before he could test that belief. Truman believed his target was purely military. Yamada vowed revenge and ended the year still not believing everything he was told. No verified diary for the surrender ceremony on 2 September is included here. That gap is left open rather than filled with memory.
calendar_note: Japanese diaries of the period are often dated by era year: Shōwa 20 is 1945, and Shōwa 19 is 1944. All dates are Gregorian. Time zones matter for the atomic missions. Tinian ran one hour ahead of Hiroshima, so Lewis's log times may not match Japanese local time. The Hiroshima attack at about 8:15 a.m. on 6 August, Japan time, fell on the evening of 5 August in Washington. Air raids that began just after midnight, such as the Tokyo raid of 9–10 March, are dated by different writers to either day. Where a diarist headed an entry with the earlier date but described events after midnight, both dates are given.

eyes.name: Kiyosawa Kiyoshi
eyes.role: Liberal journalist and diplomatic commentator, aged 54; had lived and worked in the United States as a young man
eyes.authenticity: Kept secretly from 1942 until shortly before his death on 21 May 1945, as raw material for a planned history. First published in 1948 as Ankoku nikki. English translation, edited by Eugene Soviak, published by Princeton in 1999. His daughter gave the manuscripts to Azumino City in 2013.
eyes.bio: Educated in America, Kiyosawa watched Japan's war with an outsider's scepticism and wrote down what could no longer be said aloud. He recorded rumour, propaganda and his neighbours' fatalism closely. He did not live to see the defeat he predicted.

sources.title: Kiyoshi Kiyosawa (Wikipedia)
Phyllis Birnbaum, review of A Diary of Darkness, London Review of Books
A Diary of Darkness (Project MUSE)
imidas: Ankoku nikki, April 1945 entries

eyes.name: Nagai Kafū
eyes.role: Novelist, aged 65, living alone in his Western-style house Henkikan in Azabu, Tokyo
eyes.where: Tokyo until 10 March 1945; then Akashi, Okayama and Katsuyama as a refugee
eyes.authenticity: Danchōtei nichijō, kept from 1917 until his death and published in full in his collected works. Kafū revised some entries later. A draft notebook dated 9 March 1945 was shown in an Ichikawa City exhibition. The main 1945 entries used here come from secondary Japanese summaries.
eyes.bio: Kafū had long despised the militarists. His diary blames Tokyo's ruin on the government as much as on American planes. After Henkikan burned with his library, he drifted west with friends and ended up as Tanizaki's anxious guest on the day the war ended.

sources.title: imidas: Kafū and Tanizaki diaries, August 1945
Kobe Shimbun: Kafū's nine days in Akashi, June 1945
Okayama City: Kafū's evacuation site (Shōgetsu inn)
Ichikawa City exhibition list (Danchōtei nichijō draft notebook, 9 March 1945)

eyes.name: Tanizaki Jun'ichirō
eyes.role: Novelist, aged 58, evacuated with his household to Katsuyama, Okayama Prefecture
eyes.authenticity: Wartime diary published after the war and summarised in imidas's 1945 diary series. Its entries for 13–15 August match Kafū's for the same days.
eyes.bio: Tanizaki spent the war writing his long novel Sasameyuki (The Makioka Sisters) and saying almost nothing about the war itself. His August entries, about lodging, fuel and food for Kafū and the broadcast he could not hear, show a household where the end arrived almost by accident.

sources.title: imidas: Kafū and Tanizaki diaries, August 1945

eyes.name: Uchida Hyakken
eyes.role: Essayist and humorist, aged 55, working in Tokyo
eyes.vantage_label: same city, burned out in May
eyes.authenticity: Air-raid diary published in 1955 as Tōkyō shōjin ('Tokyo Burned Out'); now a Chikuma Bunko paperback. Entries cited here follow imidas's 1945 diary series.
eyes.bio: Uchida, a disciple of Natsume Sōseki, wrote with a deadpan eye for small things: drinking with a friend called up to the navy, swallows nesting in a bombed station, a bottle of sake he would not leave behind. His records of fire are the more terrible for their calm.

sources.title: imidas: Uchida Hyakken, Tōkyō shōjin (January 1945 instalment)
Chikuma Shobō edition

eyes.name: Yamada Fūtarō (Yamada Seiya)
eyes.role: Medical student at Tokyo Medical College, aged 23; later a famous popular novelist
eyes.where: Tokyo; after 25 May with family in Tajima (Hyōgo) and Yamagata; in August at his college's evacuation site in Nagano Prefecture
eyes.vantage_label: young patriot in the burning city
eyes.authenticity: Published in 1971 as Senchūha fusen nikki ('Diary of a Non-Combatant of the War Generation'). The author said the entries for the days after his lodgings burned were reconstructed from memory on 5 June. Adapted as a manga, Fūtarō fusen nikki.
eyes.bio: Unlike the older liberal writers, Yamada began 1945 vowing to live and die for his country, and he answered the March fire with a cry for revenge. His defeat entries record a young believer's shock. At year's end he wrote that he had been a bystander who neither fought nor died.

sources.title: Kobe Shimbun on the diary and its manga adaptation
Ian Buruma, 'Ecstatic about Pearl Harbor', New York Review of Books
Chikuma Bunko edition

eyes.name: Ishikawa Kōyō
eyes.role: Photographer in the Metropolitan Police Department's photography section, aged 40
eyes.where: Police headquarters air-defence basement, then the burning Kōtō district
eyes.authenticity: Diary entries transcribed in Tōkyō daikūshū sensaishi, vol. 4 (1973), pp. 756–760, and translated by Cary Karacas. His photographs of the dead are the best-known visual record of the raid.
eyes.bio: Ishikawa was ordered to document the damage, and he did. His entry for the night of 9–10 March moves from routine darkroom work to near-death in the fire at Ryōgoku, and then to photographing corpses in Asakusa and Honjo that afternoon.

sources.title: Ishikawa Kōyō diary entries, trans. Cary Karacas (PDF)
Bodies and Structures: Documenting Destruction

eyes.name: Oki Misao
eyes.role: Chief Secretary of the House of Representatives
eyes.vantage_label: fighting the fire at the Diet
eyes.authenticity: Held in the National Diet Library's modern political archives as 'Oki's account of the war devastation of 16 May – 8 June and 14 July 1945', with an entry dated 26 May 1945.
eyes.bio: Oki's record comes from the centre of the state. While central Tokyo burned, his staff fought the fire at the parliament building, and cabinet members' families sheltered inside it.

sources.title: National Diet Library, Modern Japan in archives: the Diet building bombed

eyes.name: Leon Ma. Guerrero
eyes.role: Filipino lawyer, journalist and diplomat, aged 29, attached to the Japanese-sponsored Philippine Republic's mission in Japan
eyes.side: Philippines (Laurel government, a Japanese client state)
eyes.where: Tokyo area; after the surrender, in Allied 'technical custody' with Axis diplomats at Atami
eyes.authenticity: Entries published by the Philippine Diary Project. A postscript runs from 29 August 1945 to 4 July 1946. His exact posting in Japan needs checking against the full biography.
eyes.bio: Guerrero had fought with USAFFE before serving the Japanese-sponsored republic, an ambiguous position that gives his diary its double vision. He was a colonial subject of America living in Japan's capital, reading Japanese papers and sleeping through alarms until the bombs came close.

sources.title: Philippine Diary Project: 10 March 1945
Philippine Diary Project: 25 April 1945
About Leon Ma. Guerrero
Diary of Leon Ma. Guerrero (category)

eyes.name: Takami Jun
eyes.role: Novelist and poet, aged 38, living in Kamakura since 1943
eyes.authenticity: Part of the very long Takami Jun nikki (published 1964; more than 3,000 pages). The 1945 portion circulates as Haisen nikki ('Defeat Diary'). Donald Keene draws on it in So Lovely a Country Will Never Perish (2010).
eyes.bio: A former leftist who had renounced his views under police pressure, Takami recorded the end with mixed feelings. He had wanted Japan to win, grieved its defeat, and was ashamed that freedom came from an occupying army.

sources.title: Jun Takami (Wikipedia)
Weathernews: diarists on the weather of 15 August 1945
Donald Keene, So Lovely a Country Will Never Perish

eyes.name: Ōsaragi Jirō
eyes.role: Popular historical novelist, aged 47, living in Kamakura
eyes.authenticity: Published as Shūsen nikki ('End-of-War Diary'). The 15 August entry used here follows Weathernews's summary.
eyes.bio: Ōsaragi was Takami's neighbour in the Kamakura writers' colony. He wrote down how ordinary people took the news, including a tofu seller who had expected the broadcast to bring good news.

sources.title: Weathernews: diarists on the weather of 15 August 1945

eyes.name: Henry L. Stimson
eyes.authenticity: Typed diary, dictated nightly, held in the Stimson papers at Yale. Widely cited for the July 1945 Kyoto debate. The entry used here follows Alex Wellerstein's document transcription.
eyes.bio: Stimson had visited Kyoto in the 1920s and fought hard to take it off the target list. His diary records the arguments he used with Truman: that bombing the old capital would make postwar reconciliation harder.

sources.title: Alex Wellerstein, 'The Most Awful Responsibility' (documents)

eyes.name: Harry S. Truman
eyes.role: President of the United States, aged 61, at the Potsdam Conference
eyes.authenticity: Handwritten 'Potsdam diary', Truman Library, President's Secretary's Files (NARA ID 183568382). Rediscovered in 1979 and printed in Off the Record (1980).
eyes.bio: Truman kept irregular private notes. At Potsdam he wrote of the bomb with awe and some self-reassurance. His conviction that it would strike only soldiers and sailors is one of the record's most consequential misreadings.

sources.title: DocsTeach (National Archives): Diary note, Truman, 7/25/1945
Truman diary, 25 July 1945 (MIT course transcription)
Diaries of Note: 'The most terrible thing ever discovered'

eyes.name: Henry A. Wallace
eyes.role: US Secretary of Commerce, aged 56, former Vice President
eyes.authenticity: Wallace's diary is held at the University of Iowa, and selections were published as The Price of Vision (1973). The 10 August entry is the source for Truman's remarks to the cabinet that day, per Wellerstein.
eyes.bio: Wallace was a progressive sidelined from the vice-presidency in 1944. He recorded what Truman said in cabinet the day after Nagasaki. It is the clearest contemporary evidence that the President ordered a halt to further atomic bombing.

sources.title: Alex Wellerstein, 'The Most Awful Responsibility' (documents)

eyes.name: Robert A. Lewis
eyes.role: Captain, USAAF, aged 27; co-pilot of the B-29 Enola Gay, 509th Composite Group
eyes.where: North Field, Tinian, and aboard the Enola Gay over Hiroshima
eyes.vantage_label: in the aircraft that dropped the bomb
eyes.authenticity: Eight-page account in a War Department navigator's notebook, written at the request of New York Times reporter William Laurence. It is framed as a letter ('Dear Mom & Dad'). Some passages were added after landing, and the famous exclamation may come from those. Sold at Sotheby's (1971, 1978), Christie's (2002) and Heritage (2022); offered again in 2026. A mimeographed copy came from Capt. William Parsons' papers.
eyes.bio: Lewis, a cocky young pilot, wrote a running log of engine start, take-off, arming and release, then groped for words at what he saw. His notebook is the closest thing to a diary from inside the attack.

sources.title: Rare Book Monthly on the Lewis log
Military Times (2026): Lewis's combat notebook for sale

eyes.name: Hachiya Michihiko
eyes.role: Physician, aged 42; director of the Hiroshima Communications Hospital
eyes.where: His home about a mile from the hypocentre, then his own hospital
eyes.vantage_label: victim and physician at ground zero
eyes.authenticity: First published in the small medical journal Teishin igaku. Translated and edited by Dr. Warner Wells (ABCC) as Hiroshima Diary: The Journal of a Japanese Physician, August 6 – September 30, 1945 (UNC Press, 1955). Wells's editing means the English text should not be read as a raw daybook.
eyes.bio: Hachiya had been on night duty as an air warden and was resting at home when the blast stripped off his clothes. Badly burned himself, he became a patient in his own hospital and then its clinician. He recorded symptoms that no one yet understood as radiation sickness.

sources.title: Michihiko Hachiya (Wikipedia)
Hiroshima Diary (UNC Press)

eyes.name: Wakahara Takeo
eyes.role: Associate professor, Second Department of Pathology, Nagasaki Medical College (drafted away in April 1945)
eyes.where: Away on military service on 9 August; reconstructing events in Nagasaki afterwards
eyes.authenticity: Recollection dated 27 May 1955 for a tenth-anniversary volume of the Nagasaki Medical College, now in English on Nagasaki University's site. It is secondhand by the author's own account, based largely on survivors such as Professor Takeuchi's widow. Included because no verified dated Nagasaki diary could be confirmed for this chapter.
eyes.bio: Wakahara was not there. His account lists, department by department, who died, who disappeared and who wasted away over the following months. It stands for the many Nagasaki testimonies that were written later rather than in the moment.

sources.title: Nagasaki University Atomic Bomb Disease Institute: Second Pathology recollections (PDF)

entries.headline: Kafū blames the soldiers, not the enemy, for ruin
entries.digest: Kafū ends the year with an indictment. Japan's destruction is the work of its own military, not of foreign enemies. He wants the army's crimes written down so they cannot be forgotten. It is a dangerous thing to put on paper in wartime Tokyo.
entries.source_note: Ian Buruma, NYRB, 14 Oct 2010, summarising Keene's So Lovely a Country Will Never Perish.

entries.headline: A medical student greets the 'year of fate' under flak
entries.digest: Yamada opens the year by calling it the year of fate. Anti-aircraft guns are firing while he lies in bed, and he vows to live and die for his country. His tone is the opposite of the older writers' quiet despair.
entries.source_note: Kobe Shimbun, Aug 2021, on Senchūha fusen nikki.

entries.headline: Bad cabinet policy hurts Tokyo more than bombers
entries.digest: Kafū writes that Tokyo's people suffer more from the military-led government's policies than from the American raids. For him, the shortages, controls and forced evacuations are the deeper disaster.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, August instalment (Kafū and Tanizaki).

entries.headline: Farewell drinks for a friend bound for the navy
entries.digest: After work, Uchida visits his friend Murayama, who must report to the navy the next day. They drink beer and sake together, and Uchida walks home drunk under the moon. The war shows up here as a missing friend, not a fire.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, January instalment (Tōkyō shōjin).

entries.headline: Ueno burns; firemen cannot find the hydrants
entries.digest: After the heavy raid of 25 February, Kiyosawa notes that Ueno is burning and firefighters cannot even locate the water hydrants. He checks the bookshop district of Jinbōchō, finds it unburned, and collects books he had bought there. A dress rehearsal for March.
entries.source_note: LRB review by Phyllis Birnbaum of A Diary of Darkness (1999).

entries.headline: Strong wind, ash in the air, a night on duty
entries.digest: The day is clear with a hard wind that whips ash off already-burned districts. Ishikawa works in the darkroom enlarging prints, interrupted again and again by phone calls and messengers. Expecting a big raid, he spends the night in the air-defence basement. An alert at about 10:30 p.m. is lifted, then just after midnight reports of incendiary attacks begin to arrive.
entries.source_note: Ishikawa Kōyō diary, trans. Cary Karacas, from Tōkyō daikūshū sensaishi vol. 4 (1973), pp. 756–760.

entries.place: Ryōgoku, Asakusa, Honjo and Suzaki, Tokyo
entries.headline: Police photographer nearly dies, then photographs the dead
entries.digest: From about 12:25 a.m., low-flying B-29s set the Kōtō district ablaze. Ishikawa drives toward the fires, reaches Ryōgoku police station on foot, and nearly dies in the firestorm before finding a way out. He reaches headquarters before noon, has his eyes treated, and in the afternoon photographs the corpses of Asakusa and Honjo. At Suzaki station he finds the remains of the police chief and learns that 39 officers are dead.
entries.source_note: Ishikawa Kōyō diary, trans. Karacas (PDF on Scalar, NC State).

entries.headline: Henkikan and a lifetime's library go up in flames
entries.digest: In the small hours of 10 March, the fires reach Kafū's house in Azabu, and he flees and watches it burn with his books and papers. The date is uncertain. An Ichikawa City exhibition shows a draft notebook dated 9 March 1945, and one Japanese summary cites a follow-up entry under 11 March. In that later entry he digs his old Danchōtei seal out of the ashes and calls it the truest memento of the disaster. From here on he is a refugee.
entries.source_note: imidas August instalment (cites the 11 March entry); Ichikawa City exhibition list, item 73 (draft notebook, 9 March 1945).

entries.headline: Refugees stream past, laughing, in whatever they wore
entries.digest: Uchida watches the people fleeing the eastern districts walk past his neighbourhood. They are dressed in whatever they had on when the fire came, and some of them are laughing. He records the strangeness without comment.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, January instalment (Tōkyō shōjin).

entries.headline: Become demons of vengeance, the student writes
entries.digest: Faced with the burned city, Yamada answers with fury. Japan must kill three Americans for every Japanese killed, and the Japanese must turn themselves into demons of vengeance to survive. The entry shows that the fire hardened some young minds rather than breaking them.
entries.source_note: Ian Buruma, NYRB, 14 Oct 2010.

entries.headline: Woken by bombs after sleeping through the alarm
entries.digest: Just after midnight, explosions close by wake Guerrero's household. The lights will not work. They have slept through the alert and the alarm, having grown careless after so many false ones. The blasts are near enough to frighten them, and they dress in the dark.
entries.quote: Shortly after midnight we were awakened by explosions nearby.
entries.source_note: Philippine Diary Project, entry of 10 March 1945 (written in English; opening sentence quoted).

entries.headline: Mud-streaked couple tell him Asakusa is gone
entries.digest: On his way to a meeting of a scholarly society in central Tokyo, Kiyosawa meets a couple at Kamata Station. Their eyes are red and they are covered in mud. They tell him Asakusa has burned. Through them the catastrophe reaches him as hearsay, in the middle of an ordinary errand.
entries.source_note: LRB review, which dates it only as 'a few days' after a nearby entry; the exact day is not confirmed (date_iso is a mid-month placeholder).

entries.headline: Nobody resents the bombing: 'it's war,' they say
entries.digest: Kiyosawa is struck that his neighbours feel no anger at the American bombing of cities. When he calls it outrageous, they shrug and say that this is what war is. He finds this fatalism more disturbing than hatred.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, April instalment (Ankoku nikki).

entries.headline: Rumours fly every day; credulity is dangerous
entries.digest: Kiyosawa records a new rumour every day. He warns that the Japanese habit of believing without questioning could lead people to do anything if the rumours ever turned vicious. He is thinking of what defeat might unleash.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, April instalment.

entries.headline: 41,318 war dead enshrined at Yasukuni amid raids
entries.digest: Guerrero copies the Mainichi's account of the previous evening's ceremony at Yasukuni Shrine. The spirits of 41,318 army and navy dead, Admiral Yamamoto Isoroku among them, were enshrined. The paper insists the mood was deeply reverent despite repeated air raids. A foreigner records the official mourning in the middle of the destruction.
entries.source_note: Philippine Diary Project, entry of 25 April 1945.

entries.headline: The only answer to the army: cold indifference
entries.digest: Kafū decides that since nothing can stop the military's abuses, all he can do is stay coldly indifferent to the nation's fate. It is withdrawal, not rebellion, and he writes it down knowing it amounts to a kind of treason.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, August instalment.

entries.headline: Swallows nest in the wreck of Yotsuya station
entries.digest: Uchida notices that swallows have built nests in the bombed station at Yotsuya and are sitting on eggs. The detail is very small, and nine days later the neighbourhood around it burns.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, January instalment.

entries.headline: A bomber's belly glows with the city burning below
entries.digest: As the great raid on the western and central city begins, Uchida looks up at an enemy aircraft. Its underside is lit red by the fires on the ground. He sees the attacker made visible by the town it is destroying.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, January instalment.

entries.headline: House gone, he refuses to abandon the sake
entries.digest: Uchida's house burns. Fleeing, he will not leave a bottle of sake behind and declares it the best he has ever tasted. The joke is how he keeps his footing on the worst night of his war.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, January instalment.

entries.headline: Firefighting at the Diet; ministers' families shelter inside
entries.digest: Oki records his staff fighting fire at the parliament building after the raid of 25–26 May. Cabinet members and their families have taken refuge inside it. Even the seat of government has become an air-raid shelter.
entries.source_note: National Diet Library, Modern Japan in archives, 'Oki's account of the war devastation', entry dated 26 May 1945.

entries.headline: Burned out, he rebuilds the lost days from memory
entries.digest: Yamada's lodgings and everything in them burned in the raids of 24–25 May, and he could not keep the diary for days. Safe in Tajima, he sits down on the morning of 5 June and writes up what happened from memory. He says plainly that those entries were reconstructed.
entries.source_note: Kobe Shimbun, Aug 2021.

entries.headline: Black smoke over Suma: Kobe is burning
entries.digest: Two days after reaching Akashi, Kafū sees black smoke rising beyond the Suma coast during a morning alert as Kobe is bombed. The next day the smoke is still there. The fires he fled in Tokyo have followed him west, and four days later bombs fall near the temple itself.
entries.source_note: Kobe Shimbun (Akashi edition), Aug 2022, on Danchōtei nichijō in Akashi, 3–12 June 1945.

entries.headline: Burned out a second time, in Okayama
entries.digest: Kafū, lodging at the Shōgetsu inn in Okayama since mid-June, is caught by the B-29 raid that burned the city in the early hours of 29 June. The inn is damaged, and once again he flees with almost nothing. His diary describes the city and its people before and after the raid.
entries.source_note: Okayama City heritage page on Kafū's evacuation site. The raid date is standard; the exact entry date was not checked against the text.

entries.headline: Stimson pleads again: take Kyoto off the list
entries.digest: Stimson again presses Truman to remove Kyoto from the atomic target list. He argues that destroying the old capital would sour Japan toward the United States for a generation and push it toward the Soviets. He also records his thinking on surrender terms and the coming warning declaration, his impressions of Stalin, and a telegram giving the bombing schedule, which Truman takes as his cue.
entries.source_note: Stimson diary, 24 July 1945, as transcribed in Alex Wellerstein's documents post.

entries.headline: 'The most terrible bomb' to be used before August 10
entries.digest: Before the day's session with Stalin and Churchill, Truman confers with Mountbatten and Marshall. That night he writes about the New Mexico test: the vaporised tower, the crater, the flash seen far away. The weapon will be used against Japan before 10 August. He has told Stimson to aim at military targets, not women and children, and to spare Kyoto and Tokyo, and a warning will go out first. He is glad Hitler's people and Stalin's did not get it first.
entries.quote: the most terrible bomb in the history of the world
entries.source_note: Truman Potsdam diary, 25 July 1945, Truman Library PSF (NARA ID 183568382); DocsTeach; MIT transcription.

entries.place: Aboard the Enola Gay, Tinian to Hiroshima and back
entries.headline: Co-pilot logs the release, the flash, the cloud
entries.digest: Lewis logs engine start at 0227 and take-off at 0245, then the arming of the bomb in flight. At a time he logged as 8:16 the bomb falls, followed by a tremendous flash and, seconds later, two sharp jolts against the aircraft. The crew turn to watch a cloud climb past 30,000 feet toward 50,000, still visible hundreds of miles away. He writes it as a letter home in case the notebook is confiscated. At some point in or after the flight he adds the line that made it famous.
entries.quote: My God what have we done
entries.source_note: Rare Book Monthly and Military Times (2026) descriptions of the Lewis notebook. When the exclamation was written is uncertain.

entries.place: Home near the Communications Hospital, Hiroshima, about 1.5 km from the hypocentre
entries.headline: Stripped naked by the blast, he staggers to his hospital
entries.digest: Hachiya is resting at home after a night as an air-raid warden when the flash comes. The blast tears his clothes away, and he and his wife are badly burned. Bleeding, they make their way to the hospital he directs, where the less injured staff take care of him overnight. He has no idea what kind of weapon has struck.
entries.source_note: Hiroshima Diary (UNC Press, 1955), opening entry; summarised on Wikipedia.

entries.headline: A professor and his students die mid-lecture
entries.digest: Writing ten years later from what survivors told him, Wakahara reconstructs the end of his department. Professor Umeda was lecturing in the auditorium and died there with his students. Staff in or near the shelter lived, but the concrete building was gutted and the wooden wings and library burned. Others died in the following weeks and months, and one colleague vanished while moving the department's equipment.
entries.source_note: Nagasaki University Atomic Bomb Disease Institute, recollections of the Second Department of Pathology (memoir dated 27 May 1955; event date verified, account secondhand).

entries.headline: Truman tells cabinet: no more atomic bombs without orders
entries.digest: The day after Nagasaki, with Japan's conditional surrender offer on the table, Wallace records Truman telling the cabinet that he has ordered a stop to atomic bombing. Truman says that wiping out another city of 100,000 is too horrible to contemplate, and that he does not like the idea of killing so many children. It is the first sign that the man who wrote 'military objectives' in July now understood what the bombs had done.
entries.source_note: Henry Wallace diary, 10 August 1945, identified by Wellerstein as the source for Truman's cabinet remarks. The '100,000' and 'children' wording follows the widely cited Price of Vision text and was not re-checked this session.

entries.headline: Kafū arrives by train with his luggage
entries.digest: In the afternoon, Kafū turns up at Katsuyama by train, carrying his bags. Tanizaki's house is already full of family, so he finds his famous guest a room at an inn. The next day he explains that he can provide a room and fuel but cannot promise food.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, August instalment.

entries.headline: Can't hear the radio; learns of surrender from family
entries.digest: Tanizaki goes to a neighbour's house to hear the Emperor's broadcast but cannot make out the words. Back home, he is reading Kafū's manuscript when his family tells him Japan has surrendered. His entry notes only that the townspeople are excited and that his household is weeping.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, August instalment.

entries.headline: Rice balls for the journey, then wine for peace
entries.digest: Kafū notes the weather and his train back to Okayama. Tanizaki's wife has packed him rice balls with kelp and beef. He arrives around 2 p.m., learns that the war is over, and that evening drinks wine with friends to celebrate. Of all the eyes, he is the only one who records unmixed relief.
entries.source_note: imidas 1945 diary series, August instalment; NYRB review (celebration).

entries.headline: Told of defeat under a blazing sun
entries.digest: Takami describes a hard, eye-hurting sun overhead and cicadas shrilling in an otherwise silent town as the news of defeat comes. He takes it in as glare and noise. In the days after, he admits he had wanted Japan to win, and is ashamed that freedom has come from foreign occupiers.
entries.source_note: Weathernews (2016) on Haisen nikki; NYRB review for his post-surrender reflections.

entries.headline: The tofu seller expected good news
entries.digest: Ōsaragi records a clear day and the announcement that the Emperor will speak at noon. People seem caught completely off guard. A tofu seller tells him that some had expected a very different, hopeful message. A few streets from Takami, the same broadcast reaches a different kind of listener.
entries.source_note: Weathernews (2016) on Shūsen nikki.

entries.place: Tokyo Medical College evacuation site, Nagano Prefecture
entries.headline: 'The Empire has finally yielded': disbelief, then tears
entries.digest: After class, Yamada hears the broadcast in the dormitory. At first he insists it must be a lie, and then he breaks down when he realises it is not. He writes that the Empire has at last submitted to the enemy under a blazing sky, and that this day must never be forgotten.
entries.source_note: Kobe Shimbun, Aug 2021 (paraphrasing the 15 August entry).

entries.headline: Broadcast heard by patients in a ruined hospital
entries.digest: Still a patient-physician in his gutted hospital, Hachiya records how the staff and the burned and dying patients take the news of surrender. He notes their bewilderment and anger that the sacrifice has ended this way. This entry was not checked against the text online, so its details are given cautiously.
entries.source_note: Hiroshima Diary (1955). Exact entry and wording not checked this session.

entries.headline: Axis diplomats under Allied 'technical custody'
entries.digest: In a postscript running from late August 1945 to July 1946, Guerrero describes life at Atami with the diplomats of the defeated Axis and its client states, held in 'technical custody' as the occupation begins. The servant of a collapsed puppet government now waits on the victors' decision.
entries.source_note: Philippine Diary Project, Leon Ma. Guerrero category page (postscript 29 Aug 1945 – 4 Jul 1946). Individual entries not read.

entries.headline: The year of fate ends; he still believes nothing wholly
entries.digest: Closing the year he had opened with a vow to die for the nation, Yamada writes that the year of fate is over and that he still does not believe everything. In late December he had also called himself a mere bystander who neither fought nor died. He distrusts the old slogans and the new ones alike.
entries.source_note: Kobe Shimbun, Aug 2021.

convergences.label: Operation Meetinghouse: the great Tokyo firebombing, night of 9–10 March
convergences.note: The same night through six pairs of eyes: inside the firestorm (Ishikawa), losing a house and library (Kafū), watching refugees from an unburned district (Uchida), swearing vengeance (Yamada), woken as a foreigner (Guerrero), and hearing of it later at a railway station (Kiyosawa). Only the police photographer saw the dead up close that day.

convergences.label: The 25–26 May raid on central and western Tokyo
convergences.note: A humorist saving his sake, a student losing his lodgings and his diary, and a parliamentary official fighting fire at the Diet. The second great fire reached the neighbourhoods and institutions the March raid had spared.

convergences.label: Potsdam: the bomb, the targets, the warning
convergences.note: On consecutive nights, Stimson records arguing for Kyoto and Truman records ordering 'military objectives' and sparing Kyoto and Tokyo. One saves an old city; the other believes, wrongly, that the new weapon can be confined to soldiers.

convergences.label: Hiroshima
convergences.note: The same minute from above and below. Lewis logs times, slaps against the airframe and a cloud he can see hundreds of miles away. Hachiya, a mile from the hypocentre, finds himself naked and bleeding with no idea what has happened.

convergences.label: Nagasaki and the halt
convergences.note: The thinnest cluster, deliberately so. A pathologist's reconstruction written ten years later is set against a cabinet diary recording Truman's order to stop. The gap between them is the absence of a verified Nagasaki diary written in the moment.

convergences.label: The Jewel Voice broadcast: surrender announced
convergences.note: Two Kamakura neighbours hear the broadcast under the same sun, one in glare and cicadas, the other with a tofu seller's confusion. Tanizaki cannot hear it at all, Kafū is on a train and celebrates, Yamada denies it and then weeps, and Hachiya's burned patients are angry. Nobody hears the same broadcast in the same way.

ties.note: Kafū spent 13–15 August 1945 as Tanizaki's guest at Katsuyama. Both diaries record the same lodging arrangements, the same packed lunch and the same news.
Both belonged to the Kamakura writers' colony and recorded the same 15 August broadcast in the same town.
Stimson's 24 July entry and Truman's of 25 July record the same conversations about Kyoto, targets and the warning.
Wallace's 10 August diary is the source for what Truman told his cabinet about halting atomic bombing.
Truman's Potsdam decision ran down the chain of command to the Tinian crew. Lewis's log is that decision carried out.
The co-pilot above Hiroshima and the physician below it describe the same instant from opposite ends.
Both recorded 10 March in Tokyo, one from the firestorm in the east and the other watching its refugees reach the centre.
Uchida in Kōjimachi and Oki at the Diet in neighbouring Nagatachō were both caught in the 25–26 May fires.
Both were older liberals who blamed Japan's own militarists for the ruin. Donald Keene reads their diaries side by side in So Lovely a Country Will Never Perish.

threads_out.note: The war these diaries end began in China in 1937. Kiyosawa's and Kafū's contempt for the army goes back to that escalation, and Kiyosawa started his secret diary in 1942 because he could no longer publish his criticism of it.
Potsdam was the last Allied summit of the European war. Truman learned of the Trinity test and set the bomb's use against Japan while sitting among the ruins of Berlin.

Postwar Japanese writers measured Tokyo's ashes against Kamo no Chōmei's Hōjōki account of the Kyoto fires of the late Heian period. Hotta Yoshie's Hōjōki shiki (1970) begins with his own walk through the burned city in March 1945.
Truman (a Missouri artillery captain) and Stimson (an artillery officer at 50) both served in France in 1918. The two men deciding on the atomic bomb were veterans of the previous world war.
Burning cities runs through the whole book: Tokyo 1945 joins London 1666 and Moscow 1812. So does the habit of keeping a dangerous diary under censorship, carried on by Kiyosawa and Kafū.
